c.tagline: Nigeria's vast Yoruba metropolis of rust-red rooftops, cocoa-trade history, and its first university.

taxi.fareNote: Street and shared taxis have no meters — agree the fare before getting in. App rides (Bolt, inDrive) show an upfront price and are the easiest way to skip the haggling.

emergency.note: 112 is the national emergency line and 199 reaches police/fire; response can be slow and ambulances are scarce, so serious cases are often handled by private hospitals. Keep your hotel's and a local contact's numbers handy.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_desc: An upscale residential and commercial district built around the sprawling Bodija Market, with banks, supermarkets, and eateries; a popular, relatively convenient base for visitors wanting shops and food with easy access across the city.

Ibadan's historic commercial core, home to the landmark Cocoa House (once tropical Africa's tallest building), the vast Dugbe Market, and Lebanon Street; central and lively but congested, best for those who want to be near business and markets.

A leafy Government Reserved Area beside Agodi Gardens and the state secretariat, with quieter tree-lined streets, government offices, and older colonial-era houses; suits travelers wanting green space and calm near the centre.
A major dual-carriageway district lined with hotels, event centres, and eateries around the Obafemi Awolowo (Liberty) Stadium; one of the better areas for dining and going out after dark.

The area around the University of Ibadan, Sango, and Ajibode, full of students, bookshops, cheap restaurants, and budget lodging; youthful, affordable, and close to the campus's zoo and botanical grounds.

water.note: Piped supply is unreliable and often contaminated; stick to bottled water.

transit.hours: Danfo minibuses, korope minivans, and keke (tricycles) run roughly 6:00 AM to around 9-10:00 PM; after dark options thin out, so app rides or a private taxi are the safer bet.
transit.note: Ibadan has no metro, tram, or city bus authority; getting around means shared 'danfo' minibuses and 'korope' minivans on fixed routes, 'keke' tricycles for short hops, okada (motorbike taxis, restricted on some roads), and app-based cars (Bolt, inDrive).
transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash to the driver or conductor, typically ₦100–₦500 depending on distance; there is no transit card. Keep small naira notes handy.

air: Murtala Muhammed International Airport, Lagos (LOS) — ~2.5 hr drive, used for most international flights
bus: Intra-city danfo minibuses and korope minivans
Interstate buses to Lagos, Abuja and beyond (parks at Iwo Road, Challenge, Ojoo)
train: Lagos–Ibadan Standard Gauge Railway (Moniya station) to Lagos

transit.m: Bolt or inDrive to city center (~25-40 min)
Shared taxi/keke from Alakia junction into town
Many fly into Lagos (MMA/LOS) instead and take an intercity bus ~2.5 hr, since IBA has very few flights

tip.r: Not expected; a small 'dash' or rounding up (₦200–₦500) for good service, porters, or drivers is appreciated but never obligatory.
